sights.address: New York City Building, Flushing Meadows Corona Park, Corona, NY 11368
sights.w: Home of the Panorama of the City of New York, a 9,335 sq ft scale model of all five boroughs built for the 1964 World's Fair, with 895,000 buildings.

sights.address: Flushing Meadows Corona Park, Corona, NY 11368
sights.w: The 140-foot stainless-steel globe built for the 1964 World's Fair, ringed by fountains and the borough's most iconic landmark.
Isamu Noguchi's own museum of stone, metal and wood sculpture arranged around a serene indoor-outdoor garden he designed himself.

sights.address: 90-16 Rockaway Beach Blvd, Rockaway Beach, NY 11693
sights.w: A 5.5-mile boardwalk on the Atlantic and NYC's only legal surfing beach, with designated surf zones and taco stands along the sand.

sights.address: 22-25 Jackson Ave, Long Island City, NY 11101
sights.w: Contemporary art in a converted 1890s public school, MoMA's edgier affiliate, now free admission with rotating experimental installations.
The modest Corona home where Louis and Lucille Armstrong lived from 1943, preserved with his den intact; guided 40-minute tours only.

sights.address: 32-01 Vernon Blvd, Long Island City, NY 11106
sights.w: A former illegal dumpsite turned free waterfront sculpture park on the East River, with rotating large-scale outdoor commissions and Manhattan views.
Hands-on science museum in a 1964 World's Fair pavilion, with 450+ interactive exhibits and a large outdoor Science Playground.
Film and TV history at the historic Kaufman Astoria Studios complex, with movie artifacts, a Jim Henson gallery, and daily screenings.
Riverfront park with restored 1920s rail gantries and the landmarked 1940 Pepsi-Cola neon sign, facing the Midtown skyline across the East River.

sights.n: USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center
sights.address: Flushing Meadows Corona Park, Flushing, NY 11368
sights.w: Year-round public tennis complex and home of the US Open since 1978, anchored by 23,000-seat Arthur Ashe Stadium.

sights.address: 175-10 Cross Bay Blvd, Broad Channel, NY 11693
sights.w: A 9,000-acre National Park Service refuge of salt marsh and freshwater ponds, one of the Northeast's premier urban birding sites on the Atlantic Flyway.

sights.n: Hindu Temple Society of North America (Ganesh Temple)
sights.w: The first traditional Hindu temple in North America, built in 1977 of granite imported from India, dedicated to Lord Ganesha.
The nation's first and largest garden-apartment community, built 1914-1939 in Tudor and Mediterranean revival styles around hidden interior gardens.
A 39-acre garden with rose, herb and bee gardens and an award-winning LEED Platinum visitor center, at the edge of Flushing's Chinatown.

food.dish: grilled octopus with lemon and olive oil
food.w: Perennially packed, no-reservations Astoria taverna considered among the city's best Greek seafood; expect a wait for the charred octopus.
Michelin-recommended Flushing institution famous for delicate, broth-filled Shanghai soup dumplings pleated to order.

food.dish: arepa de choclo with white farmers cheese
food.w: The brick-and-mortar home of Maria Cano, the legendary Jackson Heights street vendor, serving sweet grilled corn arepas.
Fiery, regional Thai cooking in Elmhurst that draws citywide crowds for its panang duck, crispy pork and drunken noodles.

food.dish: No. 6 pork wontons in chili oil
food.w: Tiny cash-only Flushing counter beloved for its No. 6, a dozen tender pork wontons swimming in roasted-chili oil.
Refined Chiapas-inspired Mexican in Long Island City, a former Michelin-starred spot known for cochinita pibil and mole de Piaxtla.
A hidden Tibetan counter tucked behind a cell-phone shop, an open secret for hand-pleated momos and thukpa noodle soup.
All-vegetarian South Indian canteen in the basement of the Ganesh Temple, prized for crisp dosas, idli and sambar at bargain prices.
